title: Veteran BBC Africa correspondent Mark Doyle dies
description: British journalist Mark Doyle, best known for his reporting on conflicts in Africa in the 1990s and 2000s, has died aged 67 after a short illness.Afte
body: British journalist Mark Doyle, best known for his reporting on conflicts in Africa in the 1990s and 2000s, has died aged 67 after a short illness.After living in Africa, he joined the BBC in 1986. Doyle became East Africa correspondent in 1993 and made his mark covering the Rwandan genocide a year later.As West Africa correspondent from 1997 to 2002, he reported on Sierra Leone's brutal civil war and aftermath of Liberia's conflict.Following Doyle's death, BBC foreign editor Paul Danahar said he was a "legendary figure", as well as a" brilliant, brave, empathetic reporter".The BBC's Andrew Harding, who worked with Doyle, paid tribute to his former colleague in a 2015 article, published to mark his departure from the national broadcaster. In the piece Fergal Keane, another prominent BBC correspondent in Africa, recalled their stint in Rwanda in 1994. "He stayed longer than any of us," Keane said of Doyle. "Those who were in that awful place at that awful time will know what Mark Doyle gave for the cause of truth and for the BBC."In the same article Sir David Richards, who headed British forces struggling to stop Sierra Leone's civil war in 2000, also praised Doyle.Sir David said his reporting helped convince the UK government of the need for a robust intervention. "Hence the saving of thousands of Sierra Leonean lives that would otherwise have been at huge risk," he said.In 2004 Doyle won first prize in the UN Correspondents Association/UN Foundation Awards for his coverage of post-war Liberia.He became BBC World Affairs correspondent before retiring from the BBC in 2015.

schema.headline: Veteran BBC Africa correspondent Mark Doyle dies

title: Autopsy shows Hayden Panettiere died from overdose of fentanyl and other drugs
description: Child star Hayden Panettiere died from the toxic effects of fentanyl, Xanax and several other drugs in her system, according to an autopsy completed b
body: Child star Hayden Panettiere died from the toxic effects of fentanyl, Xanax and several other drugs in her system, according to an autopsy completed by the Greenville County Coroner's Office in South Carolina. The coroner's office said Panettiere's death was an accident and that no signs of trauma were discovered that would have contributed to her death. Panettiere died last month at the age of 36 after she was found unresponsive at a South Carolina residence. The star of US TV shows Heroes and Nashville had spoken openly about her struggles with substance abuse. The coroner's office also found methocarbamol - a prescription muscle relaxant - and quetiapine - an antipsychotic medication that is used to treat certain mental health conditions. Drugs at their fingertips, intense pressure: Why child stars fall into addictionFentanyl is a synthetic opioid that has killed hundreds of thousands of Americans over the past five years alone. The coroner's office said emergency responders had "initiated advanced cardiac life support measures; however, resuscitation efforts were unsuccessful". The US Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) was reportedly joining the local police department's investigation into the child star's death.Panettiere's ex-boyfriend, Brian Hickerson - who has admitted to abusing her - and his brother Zack were with Panettiere when emergency services came, according to a police report from the day she died.Just months before her death, Panettiere published a memoir where she discussed at length her issues with addiction and postpartum depression. Panettiere has said she was introduced to drugs around the age of 16 during a red carpet appearance for Heroes when a member of her professional team gave her something called a "happy pill" for energy."I had no idea that this was not an appropriate thing, or what door that would open for me when it came to my addiction," she told People Magazine. "As I got older, the drugs and alcohol became something I almost couldn't live without."Panettiere's brother, Jansen, died aged 28 from a heart condition. Panettiere revealed in her book that her brother also struggled with substance abuse and used heroin and cocaine leading up to his death.

schema.headline: Autopsy shows Hayden Panettiere died from overdose of fentanyl and other drugs

title: Lindsay Clancy's lawyer asks judge to investigate juror and check his phone
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Lindsay Clancy attorney Kevin Reddington made several attempts to convince the judge not to declare a mistrialByMa
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Lindsay Clancy attorney Kevin Reddington made several attempts to convince the judge not to declare a mistrialByMadeline HalpertThe defence lawyer for a Massachusetts mother accused of murdering her three children has asked a judge to investigate a juror in the case.The proceedings against Lindsay Clancy ended in a mistrial and acrimony this month after the jury failed to reach a unanimous verdict.Her attorney, Kevin Reddington, wants the court to probe mobile phone use by "Juror Doe" during deliberations as well as a questionnaire he filled out. A lawyer for Michael Desronvil, the lone juror who wanted to find Clancy guilty, said the latest defence motion was a "Looney Tunes" attack on his client for doing his civic duty. Desronvil has said there was "enough proof that she [Clancy] knew exactly what she was doing". Figure caption, Watch: Patrick Clancy says he forgives his ex-wife, LindsayWarning: This article contains distressing detailsThe juror forewoman has claimed in a media interview that Desronvil had expressed reasonable doubt about Clancy's guilt, which would require him to find her not guilty. He denies this.Clancy has not denied killing her three children, Cora, five, Dawson, three, and Callan, eight months, at the family's Massachusetts home. Her attorneys argued she was not guilty by reason of insanity, that she was struggling with postpartum psychosis at the time. Prosecutors said Clancy made a calculated decision to send her husband out of the house on an errand so she could strangle her children. In his motion filed on Friday, Reddington asked the court to look at calls and texts that "Juror Doe" made between 08:00 and 16:30 local time during all the days the jury deliberated. Image source, The Heard FoundationImage caption, Cora, five, Callan, eight months, and Dawson, three He also asked the court to examine the truthfulness of the answers the juror gave during the jury selection process, as well as his responses to prospective juror questionnaires. In a separate motion, Reddington also asked for the case against Clancy to be dismissed. Prosecutors have yet to say whether they will retry her. Facing a backlash for refusing to acquit Clancy, Desronvil has hired an attorney to represent him.The lawyer, Edward Paltzik, said in a statement on X that the "disgusting" defence motion was an attack on the US constitutional right to a fair trial."If the new normal is that jurors are going to face brutal reprisals for disagreeing with a defense attorney, you can kiss the Sixth Amendment goodbye," he wrote.Image source, @EdPaltzikImage caption, Desronvil (seen here in a photo provided by his lawyer) has said he had no doubt about Clancy's guiltSeveral jurors have said after the trial ended that they were ultimately divided 11-1 in favour of finding Clancy not criminally responsible.Desronvil said last week that he had no doubt about her guilt. "As I tried to explain different possible theories during deliberation, I kept getting cut off as if I had doubts based on the evidence presented," he said in a statement to the BBC's US partner CBS News. The jury forewoman, a retired fifth-grade teacher, said in an interview with NBC that Desronvil had admitted he had reasonable doubt, but refused to find Clancy not guilty by reason of insanity.

schema.headline: Lindsay Clancy's lawyer asks judge to investigate juror and check his phone

title: Protests as ICE agent shoots and wounds Venezuelan DoorDash driver in Texas
description: Attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch told CBS that Garcés Perez called his wife while "yelling in pain" in hospital. She told National Public Radio he was
body: Attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch told CBS that Garcés Perez called his wife while "yelling in pain" in hospital. She told National Public Radio he was in ICE custody.The Trump administration has ramped up immigration enforcement efforts and arrests during Trump's second term, sparking unrest across several US cities. The administration has defended its policies and the agency's controversial tactics as necessary for public safety and to enact Trump's campaign promise to secure the border and carry out mass deportations.The shooting in Austin on Sunday occurred just before 1300 local time, although details remain scarce. Dozens of protesters, some waving the flags of Mexico and Guatemala, gathered at the scene carrying signs demanding that ICE leave Austin.Local television outlets showed the demonstrators gathering across the street from ​a blue Toyota Corolla that ⁠sustained damage to the passenger-side door, as ICE agents stood nearby, Reuters news agency reported.Mayor Kirk Watson, a Democrat, said that Austinites have a right to know what happened and "a right to feel safe in their city" during a media briefing on Sunday."They should know the truth," he said, adding that he is pleased that the city will also be involved in the investigation.He added that ICE operations have surged in Austin in recent weeks. ICE has faced intense scrutiny after a number of deadly shootings, including the death of Houston resident Lorenzo Salgado Araujo. Salgado Araujo had not been a target of an ICE investigation, but was shot during an ICE traffic stop, according to DHS.Texas Congressman Greg Casar, a Democrat, has demanded a full and immediate independent investigation into the latest shooting and the release of body camera footage. He also demanded "accountability for any ICE officer who broke the law".Activists say that the administration has violated due process as it carries out the crackdown. Democrats have demanded reforms at the agency, including requiring immigration enforcement agents to wear body cameras and not conceal their faces.Earlier this month the US Department of Justice charged an ICE agent with lying about the non-fatal shooting of a Venezuelan migrant in Minnesota - a rare instance in which the current justice department accused a federal agent of breaking the law on the job.Earlier this week, Florida lawmaker Maria Elvira Salazar, a Republican who has spoken out against the immigration crackdown, released an advert criticising the targeting and detaining of individuals who have no criminal record. Salazar appeared on the CBS programme Face the Nation on Sunday and said that she has since spoken to the president, and believes he will keep the country on the right track."He gets it more than anybody," she said.

schema.headline: Protests as ICE agent shoots and wounds Venezuelan DoorDash driver in Texas

title: Major US outlets boycott shared Trump coverage in protest at media ban
description: Several other US outlets have also announced that they would not participate in coverage of pooled events, with some, including the New York Times and
body: Several other US outlets have also announced that they would not participate in coverage of pooled events, with some, including the New York Times and Washington Post, saying they would not share still images from Trump events on Monday.It meant there was no network TV footage of Trump boarding Air Force One or arriving in New York to attend the UN general assembly.Trump also took part in a ribbon-cutting ceremony for the new Marine One helipad on the White House South Lawn. The event was streamed on the White House site but his comments were inaudible.The president did later appear on television following a meeting with the Mayor of New York Zohran Mamdani. He told the president that all members of the media would be welcome at the press conference.Trump said: "It's interesting because, they said they were going to boycott me, but they never boycott me, so I wasn't very worried about that. Look at all that press."The pool involves media organisations sharing material to save on costs and space when broadcasting presidential events to the American public.Fox News Washington bureau chief Bryan Boughton, who currently holds a rotating role helping to organise media TV crews covering the White House, wrote in an email seen by the BBC that "effective today, the TV pool will not be covering designated as pool coverage" of Trump.The message said the move followed the White House "preventing" CNN from fulfilling its pool duties for Trump's trip to New York and that "there will be no replacement pool put in place".The three media organisations banned from the White House filed a lawsuit on Monday in US District Court in Washington.A joint statement announcing the legal action said: "Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting."Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference."

schema.headline: Major US outlets boycott shared Trump coverage in protest at media ban

title: Friedrich Merz's political crisis threatens Germany's obsession with stability
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The German chancellor's political future hangs in the balance after bruising election defeatsByKatya AdlerEur
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The German chancellor's political future hangs in the balance after bruising election defeatsByKatya AdlerEurope editorGermany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz is a political record-breaker.The problem for him is these records are overwhelmingly negative and he is at risk of losing his job over them.The problem for the EU and for Europe more broadly is this has a destabilising effect far further afield.At a paltry 13%, Merz's popularity rating is the lowest for any German chancellor since polling began. German voters' ardour for him started lower and fell faster than any of his predecessors. The former corporate lawyer is perceived by many to be arrogant and out of touch with their problems.He has only been in government for 16 months but under his chairmanship, Merz's conservative Christian Democratic Unionist (CDU) party has suffered three very poor showings in regional elections over the last couple of weeks. The state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern broke another record on Sunday according to preliminary results: Merz's conservative CDU party did not even reach the 5% threshold to enter the regional parliament.Conversely, the anti-immigration, nationalist right Alternative for Germany (AfD) - a political party Merz had promised to slash support for when he was running for CDU leadership - has performed spectacularly well. It became the biggest political faction in two out of those three recent state elections and broke another record: they have a chance at governing in one of those states, Saxony Anhalt, despite the German authorities labelling them in part anti-democratic and far-right extremist.The AfD also tops opinion polls nationally, a particularly sensitive issue for Germany after its Nazi past.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The AfD, led by Tino Chrupalla and Alice Weidel, has surged in national opinion pollsThe party rejects the far-right label. Its German name, Alternative fuer Deutschland, means Alternative for Germany. That is exactly what they say voters now want.Following this month's regional election surge in success for the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, plus its gains in Berlin - where the victors were the hard left Die Linke party - AfD co-leader Alice Weidel said on Monday that her party had effectively replaced the center-right CDU as Germany's true Volkspartei, or catch-all people's party.The AfD accuses Merz of  failing to fulfil his key election promises to improve the spluttering German economy - once seen as the financial engine of Europe - and to find workable solutions to voter fears about immigration and security on their streets.High time for political change, says the AfD.Merz's position as German chancellor certainly looks wobbly. There have been rumours for weeks of a brewing palace coup, where he would be replaced by a more popular CDU politician. Possible candidate names are swirling but no individual will stick out his or her neck in public until they know they have the backing of the party.I have reported on Germany for decades. This is a stability-obsessed country. This kind of political upheaval is deeply unusual. Even if Merz stays in post, his political clout and credibility, his room for manoeuvre inside a fractious coalition government, will be restricted.Looking uncharacteristically forlorn on Sunday evening, Merz jumped to make a televised address even before the regional election results were confirmed.He would press ahead with tax, welfare and economic reforms to bring about prosperity, he said. "Backbone, steadfastness and patience" were required.Figure caption, Why Merz is staying on as German chancellor after election 'disaster'But German patience is running thin.Voters in Germany, as across much of Europe, have repeatedly elected traditional parties of the centre-left, such as Germany's SPD party, or centre-right, like the CDU, since World War Two - but increasingly they feel let-down and frustrated as they fear for their economic future.Voter resentment really started to mount after the financial crisis of 2007/8, when these traditional parties were seen bailing out big banks, while families felt their savings and living standards dropped. Then came the 2015 migration crisis, when more than one million refugees and other migrants arrived by people-smuggler boats across the Mediterranean and made their way across Europe, often by foot, trying to settle in wealthier countries like Germany and Sweden. Germany took in one million people.Integration into German society has been mixed and Germans have been shocked and scared by a number of headline-making attacks by migrants over the years, some with a history of mental illness, others linked by the German authorities to Islamist extremist groups or ideology. In December, for example, police said they arrested five individuals suspected of plotting a Christmas market attack in Munich "based on an Islamist motive".Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 has had another scarring effect.Germans pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe. The loss of access to cheap Russian energy that German car factories and other industries relied on, plus Donald Trump's trade tariffs and aggressive economic competition from China, have had a heavy toll on this country's export-driven economy.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, As the AfD squeezes the CDU on the right, the left wing Die Linke party attracts voters elsewhere Germany is Europe's, and therefore the eurozone currency's, largest economy. It is the world's largest single donor to Ukraine right now and it is the biggest net payer into the EU budget.When Germany's finances are in trouble and the country turns inward because of a political crisis, the knock-on effect beyond its borders can be considerable.Under financial pressure, Merz has been pushing hard, along with a group of other wealthier EU countries to slash their contributions to the bloc's budget, for example.This comes at a time when the EU wants to spend more, not less, on common defence projects, migration and AI and tech.Faced with perceived threats from Russia and China, wars in the Middle East affecting energy supplies and prices, plus the unpredictability - and many in Europe say, unreliability - of the US under Trump, now is a time Europeans must stick tightly together, says Brussels.The EU is watching Merz's travails, plus the strengthening of the AfD on the right and the hard left Die Linke too, with concern.These regional German votes come at the start of bumper election season across the EU, where all the big powers - (including France, Italy, Spain and Poland - go to the polls.Nationalist, Eurosceptic, anti-immigration parties are predicted to do well. And Beijing and Moscow are watching closely.

schema.headline: Friedrich Merz's political crisis threatens Germany's obsession with stability

title: Disha Salian: Why a Bollywood celebrity manager's six-year-old death case has been reopened
description: On 4 June 2020, as a deadly wave of Covid-19 swept through India, celebrity manager Disha Salian asked her father Satish Salian to call a police helpl
body: On 4 June 2020, as a deadly wave of Covid-19 swept through India, celebrity manager Disha Salian asked her father Satish Salian to call a police helpline to check if it was safe for her to travel.She was excited about an advertising campaign she was going to shoot and showed her parents a photo of the cheque she had received as advance remuneration.As she walked out of the door, she told her parents that she would be back in two days.It was the last time the Salians saw their 28-year-old daughter alive.On the intervening night of 8 and 9 June, Satish Salian was called by the police to a hospital where he learnt that his only child was dead.Police said she had fallen from the 12th floor of a building in the western city of Mumbai.Disha's friends at the hospital said she had been drinking alcohol and fell accidentally.Police later said their investigation had shown that her death was a suicide.But earlier this month, the Bombay High Court ordered the federal police - the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) - to reopen the case and reinvestigate Disha's death.The court order came after a petition filed last year by Satish Salian, who had insisted from the start that his daughter's death was not a suicide or an accident and alleged that she was gang-raped and murdered.His allegations that some senior police officers had destroyed evidence and created a false story of suicide to protect some ministers and influential politicians who had a role in the alleged crime has made it one of India's most discussed deaths in recent years.In the order, external on 2 September, Judges Sarang V Kotwal and Ranjitsinha Raja Bhonsale criticised the police and said there were "too many glaring discrepancies" in their investigation, which was carried out in two phases over more than six years. The judges insisted that they were not holding "a mini trial" but said "the investigation carried out by the police raises more questions than it answers".They pointed out the unexplained delay in police paperwork, that no blood had been found at the spot where the body had fallen and said that the injuries mentioned in the post-mortem report did not seem consistent with a fall. "We find this difficult to accept," they wrote.One of the biggest criticisms from the court was that the police had only investigated it as a case of suspicious or unnatural death and not registered an FIR (First Information Report) - a document police have to prepare when they receive information about a crime.Satish Salian's accusations are only allegations so far, but they have formed the basis of a new investigation by the CBI, which last week registered an FIR based on a written complaint from him.The BBC has reviewed this FIR and read through the court order in the case.Summarising Satish Salian's allegations, the court order said that at the time of her death, Disha was working with Kwan Entertainment - a celebrity management company - and represented Bollywood actor Sushant Singh Rajput."She got to know about some objectionable activities of the powerful people. She gave that information to Rajput, who innocently divulged that to others. Ultimately that information reached back those people and she was murdered to silence her," it added.Rajput mourned her death in an Instagram story. "It's such devastating news. My deepest condolences to Disha's family and friends. May your soul rest in peace," he wrote.In the initial days, Disha's death went largely unnoticed until less than a week later, Rajput himself was found dead in his home.Police also ruled his death to be a case of suicide, saying he had mental health issues for which he was under treatment. But weeks later, his actress girlfriend Rhea Chakraborty was arrested following accusations from Rajput's father that she had contributed to his suicide. He also denied that his son had any mental health issues. Following outrage, Sushant's case was also handed over to the CBI which, last year, closed the case, saying he had indeed died by suicide and that neither Chakraborty nor her family had a role in his death.In the FIR Satish Salian has registered with the CBI, he has alleged that the deaths of Disha and Rajput are linked.Disha, he says, shared with the actor "incriminating and objectionable information concerning alleged drug trafficking, child abuse and other unlawful activities" involving a former minister and some others and the two intended to hold a press conference to bring it into the public domain."In order to prevent that and protect the persons involved, a well-orchestrated criminal conspiracy was hatched. The victim was gang raped and murdered, and thereafter evidence was suppressed /fabricated and a false story of suicide was created to cover up the crimes and shield the accused."In its order, the court said that registration of the FIR "does not imply any finding of guilt against anyone" and that no-one shall be treated as an accused unless the investigating officer finds "sufficient grounds to raise reasonable suspicion against them".But as the FIR names some of the state's top politicians, police officers and Bollywood actors, the case has dominated headlines in India amid allegations of misuse of political power, denials and claims of political vendetta.Sushant Singh Rajput: Mystery and voyeurism around Bollywood star's deathRhea Chakraborty: Why is Indian TV obsessed with Sushant Singh Rajput's death?Sushant Singh Rajput: Rhea Chakraborty on 'media trial' after Bollywood star's deathSatish Salian, who's been fighting for six years to get justice for his daughter, says he's felt "some peace" after the court ordered the fresh investigation into her death.Disha, he told the BBC, was "very bright, she did well in her studies and read a lot. She had a heart of gold and was very helpful. She was our only child and she loved us very much".His wife, he says, has been unable to come to terms with her tragic death and has gone into depression."I want the death penalty for those who hurt my daughter. Those who inflicted pain on her must die a painful death too. That is what justice for Disha would look like to me," he says.

schema.headline: Disha Salian: Why a Bollywood celebrity manager's six-year-old death case has been reopened

title: Japan: Four dead as Typhoon Dujuan lashes Tokyo and surrounding areas
description: Dujuan had sustained winds of 130km/h (81mph) and gusts of 194km/h.The typhoon is the latest in a series of storms in the Pacific, made more intense b
body: Dujuan had sustained winds of 130km/h (81mph) and gusts of 194km/h.The typhoon is the latest in a series of storms in the Pacific, made more intense by the "super El Niño", which has warmed the ocean, fuelling the formation of storms.Authorities had advised the public to pay attention to weather information. Dujuan, which is Japan's 25th typhoon of the year, hit in the midst of a five-day holiday and forced the cancellation of several events.Concerts scheduled for Monday at the Rock in Japan music festival were cancelled, while the Tokyo Game Show, a video game convention, also cancelled Monday's programme.Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi offered her condolences in a post on X to those who lost their lives in the typhoon, before saying she would be continuing with her scheduled trip the United States as planned."With a sense of urgency, I instructed Chief Cabinet Secretary Takehara and Minister Hosono to respond with utmost preparedness," she wrote, before saying she had boarded a flight to the US.She will be speaking at the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, and will meet with US President Donald Trump.

schema.headline: Japan: Four dead as Typhoon Dujuan lashes Tokyo and surrounding areas

title: Father admits causing the death of his son in Cyprus hotel fall
description: Foster was allowed to return to the UK for his child's funeral, on condition that he flew back to Cyprus last week for the plea hearing to take place.
body: Foster was allowed to return to the UK for his child's funeral, on condition that he flew back to Cyprus last week for the plea hearing to take place.His lawyer, Alexandros Alexandrou, said he would ask the court to lift travel restrictions so that his client can return to the UK to be with his wife and daughter until the next hearing.Paphos District Court was told in July that the boy fell through an open window when his father was holding him around his waist and swinging him from side to side.Foster decided to plead guilty to avoid a long trial and spare his family reliving the child's death in court, Alexandrou said.A long trial would mean that the man was "again a victim of this tragedy", the lawyer told the Associated Press after Tuesday's hearing."The most important thing for him is to return to his family," he said.The maximum sentence for the charge was four years in prison, but Alexandrou said the court should take previous cases into account where defendants had been fined or received a suspended sentence.In a statement given to the BBC, Alexandrou, said:  "This was a momentary lapse of attention, without any intention to cause harm, which had the most devastating and unimaginable consequences."We will now present to the court the relevant mitigating evidence and circumstances for consideration ahead of sentencing."The family have suffered "unimaginable grief" since the "horrific events" and have asked for privacy during this time, added the lawyer.

schema.headline: Father admits causing the death of his son in Cyprus hotel fall

title: Israel vs Republic of Ireland - how Uefa Nations League matches became so contentious
description: An elite-level European football match will be played on Sunday at a neutral stadium, with no 'away' fans, and reduced television coverage.That the ma
body: An elite-level European football match will be played on Sunday at a neutral stadium, with no 'away' fans, and reduced television coverage.That the match is even taking place had been in doubt - one side had to vote on a motion confirming whether or not they would participate amid significant opposition from fans, pundits and politicians.But the vote confirmed the fixture would go ahead, and now the Republic of Ireland will travel to Debrecen, Hungary, for a Uefa Nations League 'away' match against Israel, played against a backdrop of ongoing and increasingly volatile disagreement between the two countries about Israel's military offensive in Gaza.And on 4 October, the Republic of Ireland will face the same opponents in a 'home' match in Backa Topola - a small town in Serbia.No tickets have been sold to Irish fans for either fixture, and Irish public broadcaster RTE will air a stripped-back version of match coverage, with no commentators, pundits, or half-time analysis.So how did a Uefa Nations League match become one of the most contentious fixtures in football?Hungary has been deemed a suitable host nation for Israel matches because the two nations enjoy stronger diplomatic ties than those between Israel and many other European nations, and it has been willing to provide the necessary policing and security arrangements for matches to operate smoothly.The FAI decided in the summer to play its 'home' fixture against Israel at a neutral stadium, citing "operational challenges that could impact on the delivery of the game on home soil". Reports have claimed the FAI was concerned protests could prevent the match from taking place in Dublin.The FAI gave no official reason for the selection of Backa Topola, but choosing a venue in Serbia - in a town so remote - in theory renders security management easier and reduces the possibility of protest. In 2025, Serbian foreign minister Marko Duric described Israel as one of Serbia's "closest friends and strategic partners". Serbia has also purchased military equipment, including drones and missiles, from Israel in recent years.The decision to play in neutral stadiums has not curtailed opposition.Fans of various Irish clubs have demonstrated against the matches during domestic fixtures in recent weeks, and on Monday more than 160 Irish athletes signed an open letter by the Irish Sport for Palestine group urging a boycott. The signatories include boxer Tyrone McKenna and former European champion athlete Ciara Mageean.FAI CEO David Courrell said last week Uefa had rejected a request for the teams to be kept apart in future draws, director of football John Martin described the games as a "very uncomfortable situation for everyone". Manager Heimer Hallgrimsson, meanwhile, said playing the match did not constitute legitimisation of Israel's "genocide"."We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide," Hallgrimmson said. "We're playing against Israel, we're not playing with Israel."In response, the Israel Football Association accused Hallgrimsson of "ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity".The Republic of Ireland faced Israel in Women's EuroBasket qualifiers last autumn and earlier this year after "extensive deliberations".

schema.headline: Israel vs Republic of Ireland - how Uefa Nations League matches became so contentious

title: Rwanda genocide: Dr Vincent Brown first person to face UK prosecution
description: A 65-year-old doctor has appeared in court, the first person in the UK to be charged over the genocide in Rwanda in 1994.  Dr Vincent Brown, formerly
body: A 65-year-old doctor has appeared in court, the first person in the UK to be charged over the genocide in Rwanda in 1994.  Dr Vincent Brown, formerly Dr Vincent Bajinya, who is in custody, confirmed his name and address from the dock at Westminster Magistrates' Court.He was charged following a seven year British investigation into the killings.He was told he faced a charge of conduct ancillary to genocide and six offences of conduct ancillary to murder, as a crime against humanity.The case was passed to the Old Bailey for a hearing on 9 October. A bail application will be considered later on Tuesday.The 1994 killings in Rwanda lasted 100 days, during which Hutu extremists carried out a campaign of slaughter against Tutsis and other moderate Hutus.The charges against Brown relate to an alleged slaughter in the Rugenge district of Kigali between 6 April and 13 April in 1994.Brown is accused of "killing, directing or encouraging" the deaths of members of the Tutsi ethnic group, as well as intending to destroy the group "as a whole or in part."Prosecutors said he was being charged with genocide under the 2001 International Criminal Court Act and the alleged killings were "part of a widespread or systematic attack, directed against a civilian population, with knowledge of the attack."Three members of the same house were allegedly murdered, along with a taxi driver, a mother and her young son.The alleged victims were Dominique Mukurarinda, Immaculee Mukankusi, Gerasi Rurangirwa, Leandre Mbogoye, Charlotte Kamaguja and Olivier Tuyishime.Brown is a medical doctor who qualified in Rwanda in the 1980s. He later became head of the country's Department of Family Health in Kigali and lived in a suburb there with his wife and young son.In 2006 he was worked at Praxis, a London-based charity which helps refugees from places like Rwanda.He has also served on the Refugee Nurses Task Force, which was set up in 2003 to advise the UK government.Senior police officers have previously stressed the UK should not be a safe haven for alleged war criminals, and investigators have been trained in international war crimes legislation.Sam Blom-Cooper, a barrister for Brown, told the court his client denied the allegations and was intent on going in front of a jury to clear the "stains of these appalling allegations."He said the defendant had hoped for, longed for, and prayed for the best part of 20 years, for this day.""These are appalling crimes, terrible murders committed in 1994 but this is the beginning of the end for Dr Brown."Inquiries continue into other alleged genocide offences in Rwanda.

schema.headline: Rwanda genocide: Dr Vincent Brown first person to face UK prosecution

title: Eleven injured in shooting outside Turkish school
description: CCTV footage appeared to show the suspect walking through empty streets checking a shotgun, which is clearly visible. He is casually dressed and appea
body: CCTV footage appeared to show the suspect walking through empty streets checking a shotgun, which is clearly visible. He is casually dressed and appears unhurried.Later footage showed the apparent suspect, who is reportedly a student at the school, running from the scene with the weapon still in hand.  The motive behind the attack was not immediately clear. According to Turkish law, the teenager is required to appear before a court before being officially arrested. In a statement, Turkey's education ministry said the incident had "deeply saddened our nation, and our educational community in particular".It said that three national investigators from the ministry had been sent to Manisa.Two deadly school shootings in April caused outrage in Turkey and led to new security measures for the 2026-2027 academic year, including tighter gun controls. Before then, the country did not have a history of school shootings.In an attack in Kahramanmaras, a 14-year-old killed nine students aged 10 and 11, and one teacher. The gunman died at the scene.

schema.headline: Eleven injured in shooting outside Turkish school

title: Bihar molestation case: India outrage after assault of teen girl and her friend in Jamui
description: A video showing a teenaged girl being sexually assaulted and her male friend beaten by a group of men in India's Bihar state has sparked widespread ou
body: A video showing a teenaged girl being sexually assaulted and her male friend beaten by a group of men in India's Bihar state has sparked widespread outrage.The school students, both minors, were stopped in Jamui district on 19 September. Footage shared widely online shows them surrounded and repeatedly pleading to be allowed to leave.The boy is seen being slapped and pulled by his collar, while the girl is touched inappropriately and, in another clip, carried away by a man as the boy tries to intervene.Three accused, also minors, have been arrested in connection with the assault. A special investigation team has been set up to catch the other suspects.The disturbing footage has prompted anger over the harassment of the two teenagers and renewed a wider debate about the safety of women and girls in Bihar, as well as questions over the response of state authorities.The outrage intensified after Bihar minister Shravan Kumar said that "sporadic incidents keep happening" and that the government was keeping a watch on them."The world is not entirely free of crime," he said, adding that those responsible would not be allowed to escape and would face strict action.Umesh Kushwaha, of the governing Janata Dal (United), also faced criticism after referring to such cases as "isolated incidents" and contrasting the government's record with that of the previous RJD administration.Kushwaha later said his remarks had been "distorted and misrepresented" and promised action against those responsible.Police said the incident took place around 19:00 local time [13:30 GMT] on Saturday, but it came to light on Monday after the video of the assault went viral.The teenagers, both students of 10th standard, attended the same coaching institute and had gone to the area to take photographs after their classes, according to police.Jamui police chief Bishwajeet Dayal said neither of them had initially reported the incident - officers began investigating after the video circulated widely online and traced the pair using the registration number of a vehicle visible in the footage.Their statements were subsequently recorded and a case was registered following a written complaint from the girl.A case has been registered under India's stringent Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, or Pocso.Police have also invoked sections of India's criminal code covering assault or criminal force against a woman with intent to outrage her modesty, assault or criminal force with intent to disrobe, and acts carried out with a common intention.Senior police officer KS Anupam said three minors had been arrested and that investigators had established the involvement of two other people.Police have also begun action against 32 social media accounts accused of circulating footage in which the teenagers could be identified, she added.The shocking nature of the assault has provoked outrage online, with many social media users expressing horror and questioning why a group of men believed they had the right to confront two teenagers for being together.Some characterised the incident as an extreme form of "moral policing", while others tagged Bihar police and demanded strict action against the harassers.Shreyasi Singh, a Bihar minister and legislator from Jamui, told NDTV news channel, external the incident had brought "shame to society". Singh, a former international-level sport shooter, said women in Bihar were advancing in many areas but concerns about their safety persisted.She called for the remaining suspects to be arrested quickly and for strict action against those responsible.Opposition leaders, meanwhile, have seized on the case to question the state government's record on women's safety.Rahul Gandhi, MP and senior leader of India's main opposition Congress party, described the footage as "deeply disturbing" and said the incident reflected a patriarchal "belief that men could police a girl's body, movements and choices"."This is not culture. It is patriarchy," Gandhi wrote on X (formerly Twitter).Tejashwi Yadav, the opposition leader in Bihar, said the incident had left him "deeply ashamed" and accused the government of failing to ensure the safety of women and girls in the state.Members of Bihar's governing coalition have rejected the opposition's wider criticism of the state's law-and-order record and said those responsible for the attack would face strict action.India's National Commission for Women has also intervened, calling for all those involved to be identified and arrested and for an impartial investigation.The commission has asked for a report from Bihar police and urged authorities to prevent further sharing of the video clips to protect the girl's identity and privacy.The Bihar State Women's Commission has also sought information from district authorities about the action being taken in the case.

schema.headline: Bihar molestation case: India outrage after assault of teen girl and her friend in Jamui

title: Lithuania has evacuation plans in face of Russia threats, PM says
description: Lithuania's prime minister has told the BBC his country has made evacuation plans in the face of threats from Russia, but added they "will not surrend
body: Lithuania's prime minister has told the BBC his country has made evacuation plans in the face of threats from Russia, but added they "will not surrender" if attacked.Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius told Newsnight that Lithuanians feel "constantly threatened" by Russia, in part because of drones entering the nation's airspace.He told Newsnight if his country was attacked, "we will fight back... we will engage". But he said there were plans for a "variety of scenarios" and used an example of getting elderly citizens out of cities "smoothly" and avoiding traffic jams.Lithuania, a Nato member, shares a land border with the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad.Nato is thought to have several thousand troops stationed in the Baltic state, including US and German forces. Although the US is currently reviewing its deployments in Europe, Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda said on Tuesday that a new US troop rotation was on its way to his country.Sinkevičius told the BBC. "We're thinking about a variety of scenarios, not all of them are being discussed very much publicly.""We face concrete threats, not on a daily basis, but we're experiencing them and it's a true reality for us."Sinkevičius also said the UK needed a "shift in the mindset" in terms of its approach to defence, but noted that Lithuania was "closer to the border and closer to [the] threat". Last week Nato fighter pilots shot down a drone that entered Lithuania's airspace. Lithuania has experienced numerous incidents in the past year, which it describes as "hybrid attacks" and blames on neighbouring Belarus, a close Russian ally.Late on Monday night, flights were disrupted at Lithuania's main airport in the capital Vilnius, because of what the airports operator called a "hybrid attack carried out by Belarus", involving objects that appeared to resemble the shape of balloons.The president's chief adviser, Deividas Matulionis, said on Tuesday it was unclear whether the objects were balloons.Nato said that as of December last year it had more than 5,000 troops in Lithuania, but says now that it is unable to give a precise figure for the numbers stationed there.Germany - a fellow Nato ally - has pledged to send a 5,000-strong combat-ready brigade to Lithuania permanently as a response to the changing security situation in Europe. However, Nato said on Tuesday it would reach "full operational capability"  by the end of 2027.The Germany military has failed to recruit enough personnel voluntarily and is now turning to compulsory assignments to fill some positions.The majority of troops will be based in Rūdninkai, near the Suwałki Gap - a line that borders Lithuania and Poland and also links Belarus with Russia's Kaliningrad.The origins of last week's drone incident over Lithuania have not been confirmed, however Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas told Newshour that it had come from the direction of Belarus.UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said: "Thanks to the swift and professional actions of Lithuanian and Italian forces, Nato once again demonstrated our readiness to protect our airspace."We stand united, around the clock, in defence of every inch of Nato territory."Moscow did not comment on the incident.Military drone incursions have become increasingly common across Europe since the beginning of Russia's full-scale of invasion of Ukraine.Residents in Lithuania's capital Vilnius were also forced to take shelter in May after a drone alert was triggered, briefly grounding flights and rail travel.Nato jets have scrambled multiple times to shoot down stray Ukrainian drones that have crossed into fellow Baltic countries Estonia and Latvia this year.Ukraine has blamed the stray drones on Russian electronic warfare, technology designed to change the flight paths of Ukrainian drones.Lithuania, Estonia and Latvia all joined Nato in 2004, becoming signatories to the Article 5 provision that states "an armed attack against one Nato member shall be considered an attack against all members".

schema.headline: Lithuania has evacuation plans in face of Russia threats, PM says

title: Sri Lanka Easter attacks: Court finds 15 guilty over deadly bombings
description: Sri Lanka's High Court has convicted 15 men who had been charged with plotting the 2019 Easter Sunday bomb attacks that killed 270 people and injured
body: Sri Lanka's High Court has convicted 15 men who had been charged with plotting the 2019 Easter Sunday bomb attacks that killed 270 people and injured more than 500.Those found guilty include Naufer Moulavi, who prosecutors said masterminded the suicide bombings. Nine other men were acquitted.The co-ordinated blasts at three churches and three luxury hotels were the deadliest in Sri Lanka since the end of its civil war in 2009. Forty-five foreigners were among the dead.All the bombers who carried out the attacks died in the blasts. Investigators have previously blamed the bombings on Islamist extremists, and the 25 men indicted were from Sri Lanka's Muslim minority. One died in custody.The court session was adjourned before sentencing.The accused, who had been charged with more than 23,000 offences, were handcuffed in pairs and brought to the High Court in the capital Colombo in two prison buses.Most of those killed were Sri Lankans, many of whom were children.They included celebrity chef Shantha Mayadunne and her daughter, an entire young family of five, at least eight members of staff from the hotels targeted and five members of the same family from the western Sri Lankan city of Negombo.The foreigners who died included 11 Indians, eight Britons and five Americans.Among the dead there were also citizens of Australia, Bangladesh, China, Denmark, Japan, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland and Turkey.Three of Danish billionaire Anders Holch Povlsen's children died in the attack on the Shangri-La hotel, while the family had been holidaying there.In the wake of the attacks, Sri Lankan authorities pointed to a "major intelligence lapse". Its parliament heard that a tip-off from India about the attacks was not properly shared with the authorities.In 2023, the Supreme Court ordered former president Maithripala Sirisena to pay millions in compensation to the victims of the bombings, after finding him responsible for national security failures that led to the attacks.Last month, two former senior officials were sentenced to death for criminal negligence that led to the bombings. Death sentences are usually commuted to life in prison in Sri Lanka due to a decades-old moratorium on executions.For years, Sri Lankans have held regular demonstrations demanding justice for the victims of the Easter attacks.The verdict comes as a separate investigation into former intelligence chief Suresh Sallay is under way. Sallay is accused of orchestrating the bombings with Islamist extremists.The allegations echo those aired in a 2023 documentary by British broadcaster Channel 4, which heard whistleblower testimony claiming the attacks were allowed to happen to boost the popularity of the Rajapaksa family, which long dominated Sri Lankan politics.Sallay, who was arrested in February, denies the allegations. Former president Gotabaya Rajapaksa, who was elected months after the 2019 attacks, with a campaign of tackling Islamist extremism has also denied the allegations.Rajapaksa, who has been banned from leaving the country, has asked the court to prevent his potential arrest in connection with the ongoing investigations.

schema.headline: Sri Lanka Easter attacks: Court finds 15 guilty over deadly bombings
